description: Current Affairs is building Phasor, a space weather early warning dashboard that turns NASA/NOAA solar-wind data into trend detection and real time electricity-grid risk alerts for South Africa, for the Be An Earth System Trend Detective! challenge. Full stack: Next.js dashboard, ASP.NET Core backend, Python ML, optional C++ hardware node.
summary:
Imagine a solar storm knocking out the power grid. It sounds like sci-fi, but it happened in Canada in 1989, and it damaged twelve transformers in South Africa in 2003. Today, the US has a live warning system for this. Southern Africa does not.

Phasor is a space weather early warning system built for Southern Africa. Our challenge was the Earth System Trend Detective, and we took it literally. We used decades of free NASA data to spot the patterns of these storms, and built a dashboard that turns that data into a simple, real time warning.

It tells operators exactly what is at risk, from transformers and GPS navigation to hospital power, and how long they have to act before the storm hits. Phasor is not just a dashboard, it is a watchdog for the infrastructure we rely on every day.
details:
1. What does it do?

Phasor is an early warning system for solar storms. When the sun throws a massive storm at Earth, it can mess with power grids, GPS, and hospital electricity. Phasor acts like a weather radar, but for space.

It uses live satellite data from NASA and NOAA to spot a storm coming. Then, it uses artificial intelligence to predict how bad it will be. Finally, it automatically tells power grid operators, airlines, and hospitals exactly what to do to protect themselves before the storm hits. It doesn't just show them a warning; it gives them the playbook to stay safe.

2. What benefits does it have?

Right now, the US has a live warning system for solar storms, but Southern Africa does not. Phasor closes that gap.

A severe solar storm can actually melt the insides of massive power transformers, causing billions in damage and leaving entire regions without power. Phasor prevents this by telling operators to block the dangerous electrical currents before they do damage. It also protects airlines by rerouting planes away from dangerous radiation, and it protects hospitals by automatically switching them to backup power before the grid goes down.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

A massive solar storm could cost the global economy up to $2.6 trillion and take a decade to recover from. Phasor is built to protect Southern Africa specifically. Because of the ancient rock we sit on (the Kaapvaal Craton), the effects of a solar storm are actually amplified here by 4 to 10 times compared to the rest of the world.

Beyond just saving money and equipment, the biggest impact is protecting human life. Phasor keeps the lights on in hospitals, keeps food and medicine from spoiling in the cold chain, and keeps planes flying safely.

4. What tools did you use?

I built this using modern, reliable tech.

The Brains: I used Python to build the Artificial Intelligence model that predicts the storms, and C# for the main engine that calculates the grid physics.

The Look: I used Next.js and React to build the interactive dashboard that operators look at.

The Hardware: I built a physical ground sensor using a Raspberry Pi and a highly sensitive magnetometer to measure the local magnetic field in real-time.

The Data: It's all powered by free, public data from NASA (like their historical OMNIWeb archives and their DONKI event database) and NOAA.

5. How is your project creative?

Most space weather projects just show you a pretty picture of the sun or a map of the Northern Lights. Phasor is different. It takes that data and turns it into an action. It actually tells you what to do when a storm hits.

I also got creative by connecting the sky to the ground. Instead of just relying on a satellite 1.5 million kilometers away, Phasor links that satellite data to a physical sensor sitting on a desk in South Africa, proving the science works in real life.

6. What factors did I consider?

I had to think about the real world. First, I had to make sure the physics matched our specific local geology, because our rocks make the problem much worse. Second, I had to think about what happens if the internet goes down during a storm. If we lose connection to the satellites, Phasor has a built-in replay mode using historical storms so operators can still practice and test their defenses.

Finally, I thought about how everything is connected. When the power goes out, it's not just a grid problem. It's a hospital problem, a GPS problem, and a water problem. I designed Phasor to handle all of those cascading effects at once.
